t: ok so I finally tried the sourdough thing everyone keeps talking about and honestly it's way easier than I expected. you just need flour, water, salt and a starter, which I got from a neighbor. the first loaf came out kind of flat but the second one actually had decent rise and a nice crust. the trick seems to be letting it proof long enough and not being scared of a dark bake. anyway if you've been on the fence about it just go for it, worst case you end up with some slightly dense bread lol

Yes, this backpack fits a 16-inch laptop without any problems. I use it daily with a MacBook Pro 16 and there's still room for a charger, a notebook and a water bottle in the side pocket. The laptop sleeve is padded and sits slightly above the bottom of the bag, so the computer doesn't hit the ground when you set it down. The only thing I'd mention is that the zipper on the front pocket can be a little stiff at first, but it loosened up after a couple of weeks.

This weeknight chickpea curry comes together in about thirty minutes and uses mostly pantry staples. Start by sautéing an onion in a little oil until it's soft and golden, then add garlic, ginger, and your favorite curry powder and let the spices bloom for a minute. Stir in a can of crushed tomatoes and a can of coconut milk, add the drained chickpeas, and simmer until the sauce thickens. Finish with a squeeze of lime and a handful of fresh cilantro, and serve it over rice or with warm naan.

Looking back on my first year as a manager, the biggest surprise was how much of the job is simply listening. I came in thinking my value would come from making decisions quickly and having the right answers, but most of the time my team already knew what needed to happen. What they needed from me was space to think out loud, someone to remove obstacles, and occasionally a push to trust their own judgment. It took me a few awkward one-on-ones to learn to ask more questions and talk less.

The film starts slow, almost frustratingly so, but by the halfway point it had completely won me over. The lead performance is quiet and restrained in a way that makes the final act hit much harder than I expected. Not every subplot lands, and the middle section drags a bit with a romance that never really earns its screen time. Still, the cinematography is gorgeous, the score is haunting, and I found myself thinking about the ending for days afterward. Definitely worth seeing on a big screen if you can.

When you stir sugar into hot tea, it dissolves much faster than it would in cold water. That's because temperature is really a measure of how fast molecules are moving. In hot water, the water molecules are zipping around more quickly and colliding with the sugar crystals more often and with more energy, which helps break the sugar molecules away from the crystal and spread them through the liquid. Stirring helps too, because it moves dissolved sugar away from the crystal and brings fresh water into contact with it.

It wasn't pretty, but the Hawks found a way to grind out a 2-1 win on Saturday night. After falling behind early on a deflected shot, they spent most of the first half struggling to string passes together in midfield. The turning point came just after the break, when a quick throw-in caught the defense napping and Martinez slotted home the equalizer. The winner came in the 78th minute from an unlikely source, with center back Okafor rising highest on a corner to head it in.

I've started taking the long way home from work, the one that winds along the river instead of cutting through downtown. It adds maybe ten minutes to the drive, but it's the only part of the day where nobody needs anything from me. Some evenings the water is perfectly still and catches the last of the light, and other days it's gray and choppy and kind of moody. Either way, by the time I pull into the driveway I feel a little more like myself again.

Honestly the best thing you can do right now is talk to your manager before it becomes a bigger problem. I was in almost the exact same spot a couple years ago, overloaded and too stubborn to say anything, and it just made everything worse. Go in with a list of what you're working on and ask them to help you prioritize. Most decent managers would much rather hear this early than find out when something important slips. And if they react badly, that tells you something about the job too.

A new pedestrian bridge connecting the east and west banks of the river opened to the public on Monday, cutting the walk between the two neighborhoods from about twenty-five minutes to under ten. The project, which took roughly three years to complete, includes a separated bike lane, wider viewing platforms, and lighting designed to reduce glare for nearby residents. City officials said they expect the bridge to be used by several thousand people a day once the weather warms up.

People tend to imagine medieval peasants as stuck in one place their whole lives, but that's a bit of an exaggeration. Plenty of people traveled to markets, fairs, and religious sites, and some moved for work, especially after the Black Death created labor shortages and gave survivors more bargaining power. Of course, travel was slow and often dangerous, so most journeys stayed within a day or two's walk. But the idea of a completely static, isolated village life doesn't really hold up when you look at the records.
